name: Example: Determining Whether Sets are Orthogonal
problem:
Determine whether the following set is orthogonal:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065835/assets/8f316d4e8c33c1d8d087f2fb42e283169919a4cbc9c14a67792df70a447a41b9.png)
worked_solution:
If we denote the vectors in our set ${X}$ as $\{ \mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \mathbf{x}_3 \},$ we can check that ${X}$ is orthogonal by showing that 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute each dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=2\cdot (-1)+0\cdot 0+1\cdot 2=0 & ✓ \\ {x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=2\cdot 1+0\cdot (-2)+1\cdot 0=2\ne 0 & \times  \\ {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=(-1)\cdot 1+0\cdot (-2)+2\cdot 0=-1\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So ${X}$ is *not* an orthogonal set.
